data.explanation: If damage is not repaired correctly, a cell may die or eventually become cancerous. That is why repair matters.

data.prompt: Radiation can damage DNA, yet the small doses of everyday life cause no immediate illness. Which is part of the answer?

options.label: Cells are very good at repairing damage, and everyday doses are small
Everyday radiation never reaches any cell
options.note: Everyone is exposed to ionizing radiation every day, so some does reach cells.

options.label: The damage is harmless, so repair is not needed
options.note: Repair matters, because damage that is not repaired correctly can lead to a dead or cancerous cell.

data.explanation: The cells in our bodies are extremely efficient at repairing damage, and low levels of radiation do not cause immediate health effects.

data.prompt: Match each idea to what it says about a cell.

pairs.left: Cells are extremely efficient at repair

pairs.right: The cell may die or become cancerous

data.explanation: Damage comes first, repair usually follows, and only damage that is not repaired correctly causes lasting harm.

data.statement: Radio waves can damage DNA by knocking electrons out of atoms, just as X-rays can.
data.explanation: Myth. Radio waves are non-ionizing, so they cannot knock electrons out of atoms. X-rays are ionizing, and they can.

data.statement: The cells in our bodies are extremely efficient at repairing radiation damage.
data.explanation: True. Cells repair this kind of damage all the time, which is why a small everyday dose does not make anyone ill.

data.prompt: What is dose rate?

options.label: How fast a dose is received, for example in millisieverts per year
How big the dose is in total
options.note: That is the dose itself. Dose rate is about speed: the same total can arrive fast or slowly.

options.label: How far you are from the source
options.note: Distance changes the dose, but dose rate is about how fast the dose arrives.

data.explanation: Dose rate is how fast a dose is received. It is measured in units such as microsieverts per hour or millisieverts per year.

data.prompt: What can a low dose of radiation do?

options.label: Add a small increase in the chance of cancer over a lifetime
Make a person ill within hours
options.note: Immediate illness needs a very large dose in a short time. Low levels do not cause immediate health effects.

options.label: Nothing at all, at any dose
options.note: Low levels can cause a small increase in the risk of cancer over a lifetime.

data.explanation: Low levels do not cause immediate health effects, but they can add a small increase in the risk of cancer over a lifetime.

data.prompt: Why does a dose spread over a long time carry less risk?

options.label: The body has a greater chance of repairing the damage in between
The radiation gets weaker as time goes by
options.note: The reason given is repair, not the radiation getting weaker.

options.label: Slow radiation does not touch cells
options.note: It still reaches cells. The difference is that there is more time for repair.

data.explanation: If a dose is low, or delivered over a long time, the risk is lower because there is a greater likelihood of repairing the damage.

data.prompt: A person receives a very large dose in a short time. What can happen within hours?

options.label: Symptoms such as nausea and vomiting
Nothing: effects always take years
options.note: A very high dose in a short time can cause symptoms such as nausea and vomiting within hours.

options.label: The person becomes radioactive
options.note: Exposure does not make a person radioactive. The symptoms come from the damage to the body.

data.explanation: A very high radiation exposure delivered over a short period can cause symptoms such as nausea and vomiting within hours.

data.prompt: A dose that is low, or spread over a long time, carries ___ risk.
data.explanation: Repair is more likely when a dose is low or spread out, so the risk is lower.

data.prompt: Two people each receive the same total dose. One gets it all within minutes. The other gets it spread over a whole year. Who is more likely to become ill soon after?

options.label: The one who got it within minutes
The one who got it over a year

data.explanation: Your guess is not scored. The answer comes later in the lesson.

data.statement: Exposure to the low levels of radiation found in the environment does not cause immediate health effects.
data.explanation: True. It takes a very large dose in a short time to make people ill within hours.

data.statement: A small dose every day is the same as one large dose.
data.explanation: Myth. Dose rate matters. A low dose, or one spread over a long time, carries less risk because repair is more likely.

data.prompt: You move farther away from a source. What happens to the dose?

options.label: It decreases, and not just a little
No change, because radiation is everywhere
options.note: Radiation from a source gets weaker with distance. The dose decreases dramatically as you move away.

options.label: It goes up
options.note: Moving away lowers the dose.

data.explanation: The dose of radiation decreases dramatically as you increase your distance from the source.

data.prompt: Some radioactive materials are stored under water, or in concrete or lead-lined rooms. Which way is that?

options.label: Shielding: something sits between the material and people
Time: people only look at it for a moment
options.note: The water, concrete and lead are barriers. That is shielding, not a limit on time.

options.label: Distance: the material is hidden far away
options.note: The material can be close. What protects people is the water, concrete or lead in the way.

data.explanation: Water, concrete and lead are barriers between the material and people, which is shielding.

data.prompt: A worker spends less time near a source. What happens to the dose from that source?

options.label: It goes down: less time means less dose
It stays the same
options.note: Limiting the time you are exposed reduces the dose from the source.

options.label: It goes up
options.note: It is the other way round. Spending less time near a source lowers the dose.

data.explanation: Limiting the time you are exposed reduces the dose from the radiation source.

data.prompt: The three ways to lower a dose are time, distance and ___.
data.explanation: Shielding means putting something, such as lead, concrete or water, between you and the source.

data.prompt: Match each situation to the way it lowers the dose.

pairs.left: A lead apron at a dental X-ray
Spending less time near a source

data.explanation: The apron is a shield between the X-rays and the patient. Stepping away adds distance, and a shorter visit means less time.

data.statement: There is nothing a person can do to lower a dose from a source.
data.explanation: Myth. People lower a dose with less time near the source, more distance from it, and shielding between themselves and it.

data.prompt: A friend says: 'Bananas are radioactive, so eating one must make me ill.' What is a calm answer?

options.label: A banana holds a little natural radioactive potassium, and everyone gets small doses daily: the size of the dose matters
You are right: radioactive always means dangerous
options.note: Radioactive does not automatically mean dangerous. The size and the speed of the dose matter.

options.label: Bananas are not radioactive at all
options.note: A banana does hold a little natural radioactive potassium, potassium-40.

data.explanation: A banana does hold a little potassium-40, and everyone gets small natural doses every day. It is the size and the speed of a dose that matter.

data.prompt: A report says a scan gave a dose of about 10 millisieverts. How does that compare with an average year, about 6, and with about 1000?

options.label: A little more than an average year, and about a hundred times less than 1000
Far more than 1000, so a scan is dangerous
options.note: 10 is far less than 1000. About 1000 in a short time is where illness starts.

options.label: Far less than an average year
options.note: 10 is a little more than the average year's 6, not far less.

data.explanation: 10 is a little more than an average year's 6, and about a hundred times less than the 1000 where people start to become ill.

data.prompt: Two people each receive 10 millisieverts. One got it in a few minutes, the other over a whole year. Which question tells them apart?

options.label: How fast did the dose arrive?
How big was the dose?
options.note: Both received the same size, 10 millisieverts. The question that tells them apart is about speed.

options.label: Is the radiation natural?
options.note: That is a different question and does not tell these two apart.

data.explanation: The size is the same, so the difference is the dose rate: how fast the dose arrived.

data.prompt: A headline says 'Radiation found in the air!' and gives no numbers. What should you ask first?

options.label: How big is the dose, and how does it compare with an ordinary year?
Nothing: if radiation is found, it is dangerous
options.note: Radiation is around us all the time. What matters is the size and the speed of the dose.

options.label: Only whether the radiation is natural or made by people
options.note: Natural or not, the dose is what matters. Most of the average yearly dose is natural.

data.explanation: With no number, a headline cannot tell you much. Ask how big the dose is, and compare it with doses you know, like an average year.

data.prompt: Is a whole-body CT scan, about 10 millisieverts, the same kind of dose as one of about 1000 millisieverts received in a short time?

options.label: No: it is about a hundred times smaller, and size and speed both matter
Yes: radiation is radiation
options.note: A dose a hundred times bigger, arriving in a short time, is a very different step on the scale.

options.label: Yes: both make people ill within hours
options.note: Immediate illness is for a very large dose in a short time, about 1000 millisieverts, not 10.

data.explanation: 10 millisieverts is about a hundred times smaller than 1000. How big a dose is, and how fast it arrives, decide what it does.

data.prompt: Match each question to what it asks about a dose.

pairs.right: All at once, or over time
Doses you already know, like an average year

data.explanation: Size, speed and comparison are the three things that turn a bare number into something you can judge.

data.statement: Any dose of radiation, however small, is deadly.
data.explanation: Myth. Everyone gets small doses every day. It takes a very large dose in a short time, about 1000 millisieverts, to make people ill. Low doses add a small chance of cancer over a lifetime.

data.statement: A very large dose in a short time can make people ill.
data.explanation: True. About 1000 millisieverts in a short time is the threshold for acute radiation syndrome. How big a dose is, and how fast it arrives, decide what it does.

data.prompt: About what dose is the threshold for acute radiation syndrome?

options.label: About 6 millisieverts
options.note: That is an average year's dose, which is far below the threshold.

options.label: About 0.3 millisieverts
options.note: That is a year of cosmic rays at sea level, far below the threshold.

data.explanation: The dose threshold for acute radiation syndrome is about 1 sievert, or 1000 millisieverts.

data.prompt: A dentist puts a lead apron on a patient for an X-ray of the teeth. Which way is that?

options.label: Time
options.note: The apron does not shorten the X-ray. It is a barrier.

options.label: Distance
options.note: The patient does not move away. A barrier is put in the way.

data.explanation: A lead apron is a barrier between the X-ray and the rest of the patient's body: shielding.

data.prompt: Which of these can shield against penetrating gamma rays?

options.label: A sheet of paper
options.note: Paper stops alpha particles, but gamma rays pass through it. They need thick, dense material.

options.label: The top layer of skin
options.note: Skin stops alpha particles. Gamma rays are very penetrating.

data.explanation: Barriers of lead, concrete or water protect against penetrating gamma rays.

data.prompt: Why is a room with more walls between you and the outside a better shelter?

options.label: More walls give more protection from the radiation outside
Walls only keep the room warm
options.note: More walls provide more protection from radiation, not just from the cold.

options.label: Walls make the radiation quieter
options.note: Radiation makes no sound. More walls simply give more protection.

data.explanation: More walls between you and the outside provide more protection, like more shielding.

data.prompt: A worker steps back from a source to a spot much farther away. Which way is that?

options.label: Shielding
options.note: Nothing is placed between the worker and the source. The worker simply moves away.

options.label: Time
options.note: It is about where the worker stands, not how long.

data.explanation: Moving farther from the source lowers the dose: distance.

data.prompt: A whole-body CT scan is about 10 millisieverts. How does that compare with about 1000, where people start to become ill?

options.label: About the same size
options.note: Ten and a thousand are not the same size: 1000 is a hundred times 10.

options.label: About a hundred times bigger
options.note: It is the other way round: 1000 is the bigger dose.

data.explanation: 10 is a hundred times smaller than 1000, so a CT scan is a very different step on the scale.

data.statement: Everyone gets a small dose of radiation every day.
data.explanation: True. The ground, space and radon in the air each add a little, every day, to everyone.

data.prompt: Where does most of the average yearly dose come from?

options.label: Nuclear power stations
options.note: A year of living near a nuclear power station adds less than 0.01 millisieverts, a tiny share.

options.label: Mobile phones
options.note: Phones use radio waves, which are non-ionizing. Most of the yearly dose is natural background radiation.

data.explanation: Most of the average yearly dose is natural background radiation: radon, rocks and soil, and cosmic rays.

data.prompt: Of these three, which adds the most to a person's dose in a year?

options.label: Radon in an average US home, about 2.3 millisieverts
Cosmic rays at sea level, about 0.3 millisieverts
options.note: That adds about 0.3, which is less than radon's 2.3.

options.label: Living near a nuclear power station, under 0.01 millisieverts
options.note: That adds under 0.01, the smallest of the three.

data.explanation: Radon in an average US home adds about 2.3 millisieverts a year, cosmic rays at sea level about 0.3, and living near a nuclear power station under 0.01.

data.statement: Ionizing radiation can damage the DNA in a cell.
data.explanation: True. It has enough energy to affect the atoms in living cells, and so it can damage their genetic material, DNA.

data.statement: About 99 in 100 people given a one-time dose of 100 millisieverts would not get cancer as a result.
data.explanation: True. The EPA says about 99 percent would not, and that at this dose extra cancers caused by radiation would be extremely difficult to identify.

data.statement: A radiation number with no unit and nothing to compare it with tells you whether a dose is large.
data.explanation: Myth. Without a unit and a comparison, such as an average year of about 6 millisieverts, a number cannot tell you whether a dose is large.

data.statement: A year of living near a nuclear power station gives a bigger dose than one whole-body CT scan.
data.explanation: Myth. A year near a nuclear power station adds under 0.01 millisieverts. One whole-body CT scan is about 10.

data.statement: Effects of radiation are more severe at higher doses and at higher dose rates.
data.explanation: True. A bigger dose, or the same dose arriving faster, gives more severe effects.

data.statement: The cells in our bodies are very good at repairing damage from radiation.
data.explanation: True. The cells in our bodies are extremely efficient at repairing this damage.

data.statement: A low dose can add a small increase in the risk of cancer, but it is not a certainty.
data.explanation: True. Low levels can cause a small increase in the risk of cancer over a lifetime. That is a small chance, not a certainty.

data.prompt: Why can ionizing radiation damage a cell?

options.label: It has enough energy to affect the atoms in the cell
It makes the cell radioactive
options.note: Exposure does not make anything radioactive. The damage comes from what the radiation does to atoms.

options.label: It is much bigger than a cell
options.note: Size is not the reason. Ionizing radiation has enough energy to affect atoms.

data.explanation: Ionizing radiation has enough energy to affect the atoms in living cells, and that is how it damages their DNA.
